speechtext: Therefore you did not say it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Coming to the budget, I should like to comment briefly on the remarks made last night by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). About half way down the left-hand column on page 2559 of Hansard the hon. member is reported in these words:
Farm income is up from $1,300 per farm in 1939 to $3,800 per farm in 1948.
He omitted any reference to the cost of farm machinery, to the cost of lumber to build a house or to repair buildings; he omitted any mention whatsoever of the increased cost of living. But even had the cost of production and living remained the same as in 1939, it was still not out of line or out of order to increase farm income in this country on an average from $1,300 to $3,800 per year, because anyone who reads the figures produced by the bureau of statistics and by other organizations knows that these figures are not net to the farmer; these are gross income figures.
Anyone who brags about an increase from practically no income-$1,300-to $3,800 is not doing a service to agriculture in this country. He is a babe in the woods-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The only point I made there was that the only standard by which these things could be judged is the fact that the average farm income between 1939 and 1948 has trebled. Everyone knows that the cost of living or the cost of agricultural machinery has not been trebled in the same period or anything near it. I was simply trying to show that this government has made real progress, despite the gloomy forecast made by hon. members of the C.C.F. in 1945.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not a point of order; it is another speech. I do not blame the hon. member; but I do not think I should permit him to proceed further, because I would prefer to finish what I have to say. The hon. member rose to a point of order, and then proceeded to make a short speech.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And I will make another-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not during my time. You may later, if Mr. Speaker will permit you.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You had better not mention my speech, then.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is no credit coming to any government which claims that it has raised income from nothing, or practically nothing, to $3,800 a year. What I am trying to say is that agriculture has still not had anything like its share of the national income.
In this connection let me place on record some figures given by the Canadian Federa-
The Budget-Mr. Bentley tion of Agriculture, as they appear in the second to last issue of the Alberta wheat pool budget, page 3. They say that for the years 1931 to 1936 inclusive there was a net loss of from 4-0 to 7-0 on invested capital in the agricultural industry of this country. There continued to be a net loss during the following years from 1937 to 1941 on investment returns of from 3-9 in 1937 to 4-7 in 1941, inclusive. Here is something to remember; during the period from 1937 to 1941 the companies which handled, processed and sold food had a return on their investment of anywhere from 6-7 per cent to 10-9 per cent during the period 1937 to 1941. During the time the primary producers of foodstuffs were losing money on their investment the handlers were making money; and during the greater part of that period there was no war. In this country a Liberal government could have given serious consideration to adjusting the economic factors so as to reverse that condition.
Is it any wonder that the farmers had incomes of only $1,300 a year in the first year mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver North? The picture changed slightly, so that the farmers received a small return on their investment in the years 1942, 1943 and 1944. In 1945 however they again had a slight loss. During those years every one of these food handling companies had definite returns of from 7-4 per cent to 9-9 per cent. Taking the period from 1937 to 1947 the returns to food handling and processing companies go from a low of 6-7 per cent to a high of 10-9 per cent, whereas only in a few years of that period of time did the farmers receive any return on their average investment.
Figures showing average returns for farmers are misleading, because even with the mechanization of farms many farmers do not receive anything like the average mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver North or the figures I have just mentioned. Only a few in the higher brackets help to bring the average to anywhere near speaking distance.
However, those were not the principal points I had in mind today when I rose to take part in this debate. What I had intended to deal with is something close to my heart, namely co-operative institutions. There has been no mention whatever in the budget of any relief whatsoever from the iniquitous legislation in operation for three years in connection with co-operative institutions. No consideration has been given to the representations of these co-operative organizations. Every member of the House of Commons I am sure has received a memorandum addressed to all members of parliament under

The Budget-Mr. Bentley date of April 23 from the Co-operative Union of Canada. This is a summary of a brief presented to the government on April 4, some two weeks after the budget was announced.
For years these people have been asking for a federal co-operative act which would clarify all co-operative operations in this country. It will be remembered that not quite a year ago, in the 1948 session, the house passed a private bill to establish the Canadian Co-operative Processors Limited-I always refer to them as the horse co-op. They had to come here to get a special act of parliament; and they got it.
There is no reason why one act could not be passed to give every co-operative organization the operations of which extend across provincial borders the same type of legislation. This act would govern their procedure, and that is what the co-operative union has asked for. Might I add that the union speaks not only for the Co-operative Union of Canada, but for le conseil Canadien de la co-operation. This last named organization will be known to anyone who understands anything about co-operative enterprises in Canada. There are already three of that type of organization, besides the one I mentioned, that apparently cross provincial borders. There is the Maritime Co-operative Services Limited, the Interprovincial Co-operatives Limited and the Canadian Co-operatives Limited. There is no reason why this government should not give consideration to the matter, nor is there any reason why it should not place on the order paper this year an act such as that asked for by the Co-operative Union of Canada.
As an indication of why I think this government has not done what it should have done, I would point out that hardly ever is cooperation mentioned in this House of Commons but the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) gets up and makes a pompous speech about how the Liberals of Saskatchewan made the co-operatives. I have disputed that time and time again. I have told the minister where he is wrong. I know the history of co-operatives as well as he does, but he insists upon pinning all kinds of medals upon himself, even those found around the stockyards, by claiming that he is the father of the co-operatives. If he wants to make that claim stick by concrete action, why has he not convinced the members of the government, most of whom do not know anything about co-operation in any form, that he has something on the ball and it is necessary to have an act of this kind. He has failed completely to do that.
The result is that every time a co-operative association wishes to do business outside the borders of a particular province it must come

down here with its hat in its hand to ask permission. Expensive counsel must be sent down here to do the necessary work and it costs a tremendous amount of money before an act is finally put through to give that one co-operative the right to operate outside its own province. One act would do the same thing for all.
Nothing has been done for co-operatives in this budget by way of removing what I consider to be the most iniquitous tax in this country. I have said that before and I say it again. Any time a group of people are prepared to organize themselves into a cooperative and say to themselves, "We will do business for ourselves in a non-profit way," the government prohibits that by legislation and by doing so commits an iniquitous act.
These people do not complain about paying income tax on that part of their business that is done with people who are not members of their co-operative, but they claim that when they are ready to do business as a co-operative association at cost by the patronage dividend method, there is no reason why they should not be permitted to do it. Yet the government steps in and imposes a three per cent tax.
I should like to tell the house what has happened in connection with thirty-two little co-operatives in my district. Some of these are quite small, only handle bulk materials like fuel, wood, coal, possibly some binder twine and other stuff that is easy to handle and does not require very much labour. There are larger co-operatives that do quite an extensive business, but I am referring to these thirty-two small co-operatives around Swift Current. In 1947 their tax amounted to $4,500, an average of $141 each. Some of them hardly had net earnings of that amount. The amount collected by the government would not pay the cost of collection.
The government is determined to do nothing to offend private business in this country. They have told these little people that they cannot do business as co-operatives until they submit to the tax laws of this country and pay an income tax on the amount of capital employed. I think the word I have used to describe this sort of action is right. If I were given to using unparliamentary language I would use words different from what I have.
The government has had ample assistance from our Progressive Conservative friends in carrying out this program. I am sorry the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) is not in his seat because I intend to refer to a speech he made on March 31 when speaking on the budget, as reported on page 2221 of Hansard. He was there quoting from the remarks of Dr. Karl D. Butler of Washington, president

of the American Institution of Co-operation, as reported in the Rural Co-operator, as follows:
Both co-operatives and other business enterprises emphasize the profit motive as the principal business incentive.
I do not deny to the hon. member for Souris the right to believe that nor am I denying to Dr. Karl Butler the right to come up here and say it, but I do emphatically deny every single word in Dr. Butler's statement, even though it may be believed by the hon. member for Souris. I am going to present some evidence in support of my statement.
I do not think there would be anyone in this house who would have the courage to say that the co-operative institutions of Canada are not based on the Rochdale principle. I know that there are not many who know anything about it. There are very few members of the Progressive Conservative or Liberal parties who know anything about it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know as much about it as the hon. member.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I said that there were very few. If the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) knows something about it at least I will be talking to one hon. member who has an intelligent understanding of what I am saying. While there are very few who understand it I do not think any would be ready to go into the country and say that they do not believe in it. They know that the co-operative people of this country base their operations on the principles of the Rochdale pioneers. I should like to quote from the Fundamentals of Consumer Cooperation by V. S. Alanne, published by the Northern States Co-operative League of Minneapolis, Minnesota. Dr. Butler can deal with these people by making the kind of statement he has made, but up here he will have to deal with those who know something about it. I quote:
Here is a significant clause in the now famous program of the Rochdale pioneers: "That, as soon as practicable, this society shall proceed to arrange the powers of production, distribution, education and government; or, in other words, to establish a self-supporting home colony of united interests, or assist other societies in establishing such colonies."
There is a whole book of that sort of thing, every word of which would be useful. The statement made by Dr. Karl Butler will be denied by a great many co-operative people in this country. The profit motive is not the principal incentive. Their motive is to reduce costs and provide the best service possible and give the fairest weights without profit. That is the basic policy and philosophy of the co-operatives of this country.
The Budget-Mr. Bentley
I have some further evidence to present along these lines. I have here a brief which was presented by the Co-operative Union of Saskatchewan to the government of Saskatchewan on January 12, 1949. I know there are some people in Saskatchewan and other places who would like to create a division between those in Saskatchewan who operate co-operative enterprises and the C.C.F. This is the brief that was presented to the government in an effort to establish what these people believe is the basis of relationship between the two functions, to set out where the one could function and where the other could function. They have indicated what they believe is the basic philosophy of co-operative enterprise. For instance, on page 3 they say:
Laws in capitalistic society were primarily made to protect the entrepreneur and were developed and amended through time to protect greater aggregations of capital. While provision was made from time to time to enable co-operatives to enter the commercial field, it was always as a distinct and peculiar division of business and not as part of the general economy.
At page 4 they have this to say:
The co-operative movement grew up as a voluntary organization within the framework of a capitalistic economy.
Later on there is a fairly extensive quotation which I wish to give. They are dealing with what has happened under the Labour government in Great Britain, and they say:
If the foregoing is true in Britain, it is equally so here in Saskatchewan.
They were pointing out where the government's field was and where the co-operatives' field was. They say:
It is submitted that the co-operative movement- consumer, producer, and service-can make an important contribution to stability and the maintenance of effective and responsible democracy in a planned economy as projected by the present provincial government. Having as its base a broad democratic foundation amongst farmers, urban workers, and the professions, it at all times promotes and encourages active participation by the people in the responsibilities of political and economic ownership and control. It is real "free enterprise" in that it enables all men and women, regardless of financial investment, to enter the business field in their own behalf, and at the same time develops a social outlook in working together for service, impossible where profit is the motive.
If the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) ever gets around to reading Hansard of this day I should like him to remember those words, and then cogitate again on the immaturity of his statement in believing the word of somebody from somewhere else who was simply expressing a personal opinion, and who would have been heartily disagreed with by the great bulk of co-operators in this country.

The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker
If I ever say anything that impresses the government I should like this to be it. If they believe in their hearts that they are trying to build a democratic country in Canada, that they are trying to extend to people in all walks of life, in the political field, in the production field, in the servicing or distribution field, in the business world, the elements of democracy in which we believe so much, then I say to them that they cannot do it if, every time a democratic organization threatens the power and monopoly of some established institution, they do not extend that democracy and clamp down some particular type of legislation on the statute books of this country which will prevent the fulfilment of the purposes of these democratic organizations that rise up in any one of these fields.
If they cannot see that, then there is one other course they are going to follow, just as sure as day follows night. It is now established on the statute books that there can be no such thing as a non-profit co-operative organization in this country inasmuch as they have imposed a three per cent tax. Some day they will come to the conclusion that is not enough to do the job they want done, which is to kill the co-operatives. They will listen to the persuasion of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, and their other big friends, and they will proceed to raise the tax to five per cent. If that does not do the trick they will raise it to whatever percentage is necessary to kill these democratic commercial institutions. If they want to go in the other direction they can move to remove the three per cent tax, and they can do that right now on the budget resolutions. They do not even need to wait until those resolutions are voted upon. The government will receive the support of a great many people in this country, if not politically at least spiritually, if they will have the courage and the decency to give co-operatives the kind of treatment that they have a right to in Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My first words must be words of congratulation to the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Boucher) on the maiden speech which he delivered this afternoon. While not in agreement with part of what he said, I think it is one of the finer amenities of public life that parliament should recognize the contributions made by hon. members of other political parties. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I extend to him my congratulations on his contribution today.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the lecture just read to the house by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley).

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I rise on a point of order. I read nothing except my quotations.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I said my hon. friend read a lecture; even if he spoke it he still read a lecture. He spoke, in the usual disparaging tones, of all those who believe in free enterprise. He mentioned the development of co-operatives and intimated to other members of the house that they knew nothing of the Rochdale co-operatives, the foundation of the co-operative system. I point out to him that in 1931 when the great pool organizations, the great co-operatives dealing with the sale of wheat, found themselves in grave difficulties it was governments such as the government of the late Viscount Bennett, the government of Manitoba then under Mr. Bracken, the co-operative government of Saskatchewan, the U.F.A. government of the province of Alberta, that assured that these co-operatives were maintained and placed in a position where they might make their contribution to securing for the western farmer the largest possible return for his wheat.
I listened with no little interest as he referred in the usual manner to profits, in line with the viewpoint always expressed by the C.C.F. party, in favour of production for use and not for profit. As he spoke I thought it might be of some interest to the house to have a general picture of the development of government-owned enterprises in Saskatchewan. I am not going into full particulars this afternoon, but I remember well, as you have so often heard, Mr. Speaker, the beautiful picture that was painted of social security provided without taxation as a result of the operation of business concerns by the government of Saskatchewan, and the profits made thereby. We do not hear so much about that any more.
We used to be told of the wonders of New Zealand, but now in our own country we have a government that went into competitive business at a very fast rate indeed, and seems now to be going out of business almost as quickly. I am going to refer for a moment, before I deal with the budget references that I intend to make, to some of the concerns operated by the government of Saskatchewan out of which we were told that social security would be provided. As regards industries that are peculiarly fitted for public ownership, such as power and the like, the same trend has taken place in Saskatchewan as everywhere else under other governments, but wherever the government of Saskatchewan has entered into any industry that depends upon competition with private industry the result has been loss to the people of the province of Saskatchewan. The government went into the woollen business. They started a woollen mill, which was established

in 1945. Up to December 31, 1948, it lost a total of $147,203; and it had an advance from the provincial government by way of capital amounting to $125,000, upon which it paid no interest or the loss would have been greater. They went into the tannery business in April, 1946, operating the only tannery in Saskatchewan. To the end of December, 1948, the loss was $78,500. They were attracted to the opportunity which was offered in the shoe business. Everybody wanted shoes, and we had the raw material available in Saskatchewan with which to make shoes; so they went into business. There was a capital advance of $171,000; and the net loss to December 31, 1948, was $63,000. They found it impossible to carry on at a profit, and in December the tannery and shoe factory were closed and will remain closed until spring. The employees of these two businesses were left either to secure positions elsewhere or to live on unemployment insurance furnished by the federal authorities. They went into the brick business, and the loss to the end of December, 1948, was $28,000. They established a fish board, and to the end of December, 1948, lost $197,123. In every case I have mentioned no interest has been allowed on capital advances, which amounted to $846,650 as far as the fish business was concerned.
I mention these businesses for the purpose of placing before the house one matter, and it is this. Governments in competitive business are always hopeful of success, but in almost every case are unable to carry on profitably. I say that because we in this country must realize that social security can and must be furnished; but when it is furnished it must be paid for from the taxation levied upon the people as a whole. We believe in social security. We believe in a great social security plan under which men and women of this country, during the period of their earning capacity, will be able to contribute to a fund so that security may be assured them when they arrive at a period of life when they need assistance. When they tell me, Mr. Speaker, that government can succeed in business, let them look at the experimental station in the province of Saskatchewan where improvements have been made in social security, which I admit, but where taxation has increased by $17.50 per year for every man, woman and child in the province.
I got into this discussion, sir, because of the attitude taken by my hon. friend. From great heights he looks down upon the rest of us, the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and other hon. members in this house including myself; he impugns our motives, ridicules our intentions and at the same time places himself on a pedestal as possessing all the
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker political and personal proprieties that Providence has not vouchsafed the rest of us in this house.
Now I come to another matter; I am going to refer to the situation created by the government as a result of the announcement by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) last evening that an election will be held, presumably on June 27.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have never seen such optimism expressed on all sides. We are all glad there is going to be an election this summer in order to give the Canadian people an opportunity of passing judgment upon those of us who have been representing them in this house during the last few years. I can see the ministers going through the country-my smiling friends the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), along with the Prime Minister-telling the people of this nation, "The reason we did not serve up the menu set out in the speech from the throne is that the opposition prevented us from doing so." I look back to January 26, when His Excellency had placed in his mouth the promises of the government, as to what they intended to do. I shall refer to some of those promises now, for they will remain only promises, hopes and dreams of what might have been.
The government has had every opportunity to bring in all the legislation it chose. Every whit of legislation that was placed before parliament prior to the Easter adjournment was passed. Every item in the nature of emergency legislation that had to be passed before March 31 was passed by parliament. Here are a few of the things that the speech from the throne shows as of immediate moment, which were to be submitted at the present session. Amendments to the Supreme Court Act to abolish appeals to the privy council; approval of the agreement for the development of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence waterway. Will the government explain the situation in regard to that matter? Then there is the question of trade, one of the most serious problems affecting the people of this nation at this time. There is not a farmer in Canada who is not fearful of the situation with respect to agricultural markets; yet here we are going into an election with the government having done nothing and, equally serious, having given the people of this country no indication of their realization of the serious existing situation or of any attempted solution of the problem.
Then there is the matter of prices. Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, when the committee on prices was set up, having as its distin-

The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker guished chairman my hon. friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare? It sat for more than four months; and the longer it sat the higher went prices. Then the government decided to set up a royal commission on prices, which also sat for several months and finally evolved a report. According to the speech from the throne, the report of the royal commission was to be laid before parliament. It was tabled in parliament but no opportunity was given to the members of this parliament to place before the government and the country certain matters which would result in a reduction in the present high prices.
Last evening the member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) told us all that this government had done. He spoke of prosperity. He did not tell you, however, that under this government we have the highest prices in Canadian history and nothing is done about it. The reductions in income taxation in the budget do not go far enough. I do not see any realization on the part of the people that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), to use the words of one member, is a Santa Claus. They know he gives them nothing back; he is only talcing less during this year. With prices at the present level should not something have been done to reduce the sales tax on necessities which in the main rests upon people in the lower income tax brackets.
Another thing that was promised in the speech from the throne was the amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Where are those amendments? Did they exist? Or is it like the questioii posed by the member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) that would have been asked yesterday by the member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) if the member for Lake Centre had not preceded him. Where are those amendments? Everywhere in Saskatchewan today, the people of that province are faced with a drought the like of which has not been experienced in fifteen years. They want amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act reducing the areas of qualification. In practically every mail they ask, What are you doing about this matter? Will you bring in the amendments? Will you do your part so that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act will maintain many of us on the land who otherwise are likely to be driven from the land this year because of grasshopper infestation and drought? Produce those amendments, I say to the government.
Now hour by hour legislation is being rushed through. The order paper is cluttered, but for a long time there was very little on it. Bring in those amendments so that the people in western Canada may be assured of that hope that is being denied to them because the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is administered

under some bureaucratic regulations contrary to the principle of that law. Agricultural markets are being lost. Britain is turning to the various countries in Europe. We have three contracts with the United Kingdom for agricultural products whereas at one time we had twenty-two.
One of the sources of collective power in the House of Commons in so far as farm problems are concerned is the committee on agriculture. Why was it not set up? Why was that committee, representative of all parties in the house, denied an opportunity this session to make some contribution by suggesting alternative markets for Canadian products? Mention was made by the member for Grey North (Mr. Case) of radio broadcasting. Why was that committee not set up? Were political considerations, or the prospect of an election, the reason that two of the most important committees of this house have been denied an opportunity to function for the benefit of this country?
Everywhere communism is threatening us. Within the last few days there has been an indictment of the government in the discovery of a self-confessed spy who entered our country under the guise of an immigrant. Communism is undermining our nation in various places. Ask the mounted police. Why not introduce legislation in keeping with recent remarks of a minister of the crown that teeth would be put in the law in order to preserve this nation from the undermining influences of this heathen philosophy? Nothing has been done. Nothing effective has been done by the public accounts committee set up a few days before the recess. Now, all opportunity of looking over the expenditures has been denied by the action of this government. Why were these committees not set up earlier? Do my hon. friends opposite say there have been no extravagant expenditures? I wait for one of them to say no.

It is six o'clock and so I will go on from this point after recess.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at seven-thirty o'clock. PRIVATE BILLS

The house in committee on Bill No. 25, respecting the Globe Printing Company, Mr. Golding in the chair.

On section 1-Real estate limited.

Mr. Chairman, on introducing this legislation, as recorded on page 2127 of Hansard, the hon. member for Peel said at page 2128:
So far as I know there Is nothing contentious or complicated in this proposal, so X would ask that the bill be given second reading and referred to the appropriate committee of the house for further study.
I do not know whether there is anything contentious about it or not, but one could not help being struck by the significance of the fact that it was at least coincidental that the bill was introduced at the same time that certain legislation was being introduced, and I believe afterwards passed, in the Ontario legislature.
The Globe Printing Company applied at that particular time for an increase in what is termed annual value. I, who am a tyro in these matters, discovered from the counsel of the company in committee that that simply was a term synonymous with rental value. It is, I think, odd on the face of it that the tremendous increase in that annual value should be asked for at once; that is to say, an increase in the rental value from $30,000 to $100,000. Let us be candid about what one might fear from this legislation, combined with the legislation which has been passed in the Ontario legislature.
I put certain questions to the counsel for the company in committee, and although I missed the second meeting of the committee I am informed that the counsel for the company did not procure, nor did he submit at the second meeting of the committee, the information for which I had asked.
To go back to what one might fear from this bill, I would say it is well known that the Globe and Mail in the city of Toronto is the only firm which would be interested enough and which would have the necessary capital to take over the building and the ownership of another newspaper published in that city. The bill itself does look innocent, and as I said before I do think that the hon. member's speech was perfectly innocent also. He has assured me that that is so and that the bill is just what it states on the face of it. That assurance I shall cheerfully accept so far as he personally is concerned.
The history of the Globe company was detailed by the hon. member for Peel. There are certain facts which one can find from the statutes. For instance, the Globe company was first incorporated in 1866-that is, before confederation-by a statute of the then province of Canada. At that time the capital stock was fixed at $300,000, and the annual value of the real estate which the company may hold should not exceed $5,000. In the year 29087-164
Globe Printing Company 1877 the act was amended and it was provided that the company might by bylaw increase its capitalization to any amount which it considered requisite. In 1892 the act was further amended. There was no legislation at that the company might by bylaw increase capital stock, but it was provided in 1892 that the company could hold real estate of an annual value not exceeding $30,000.
I understand from the answers of counsel of the company that the purpose of this increase is to purchase the property in which the paper has been operating but which, up to the present time, as I understand it, it has not owned. I think that is the property of the old Mail. I asked counsel a question in committee. For example I asked him, if the company changed its mind about using its present premises, whether there was anything which would legally prevent the company from investing its increased money in other premises where it could carry on its business. He told me that legally there was no such prevention, but he also maintained that the company had no such intention; that it was perfectly content to stay where it was. They wanted to get the property and the paper under the same name and owner.
In 1911 the act of incorporation was again amended with respect to the capitalization of the company. The legislation of 1877 which put no limit on the amount of authorized capital was repealed and in that amendment it was provided that the directors might increase the capital stock but not to exceed $1 million.
The situation is now that the company can issue stock to an amount not exceeding $6 million, and it can hold real property, the annual or rental value of which-I presume the terms are synonymous-cannot exceed $30,000. It is the increase of $30,000 to $100,000 for which the company is now having this legislation introduced in the House of Commons. I think that the passage of this legislation should be delayed. While in committee we heard a brief presented by a most able lawyer acting on behalf of the company, I believe we should have something on the other side of the question. We should not be rushed into this extensive capitalization, or this increase in capitalization. We would want to know how it has been computed, or whether it fluctuates or remains fixed.
I should like to know the assessed value upon which these people pay taxes; I should like to know the value of these properties from time to time, as the years have gone by. It seems strange why, if this company has been able to carry on at all at a rental value of $30,000, there should be this immediate and urgent necessity at one jump to increase that value to $100,000.

Globe Printing Company
I believe that perhaps the reasons they have come to parliament for this amendment of the act of incorporation are proof in themselves that parliament should know why this increase is required. Some full disclosure should be made by the company as to the annual value of the property when they took it over. We could then compare that figure with this $30,000 annual value. I believe it would be discovered that the company is asking for a much greater increase than is justified.
That, sir, is my argument in the matter. I think we should have more information. I am not suggesting anything sinister, but I am merely pointing out that there is a coincidence. We should have both sides of the question before we tackle this problem or embark upon legislation for which the city of Toronto and certain elements of the press in that city may be sorry before the thing is finished.
Is the purpose of this enlarged capacity for holding real estate to make possible the purchase of any real estate that they do not hold already? The answer given by counsel was, no. He reiterated that it was simply to have under the name of the company the property they already hold and operate. When I asked if there was anything to prevent their changing that property, or investing the extra capitalization in another property, he said that so far as he knew there was nothing legally to prevent it.
Does the bill in any way permit the purchase of real estate other than that now in possession of the company? The answer to that is, apparently, yes.
Does the bill specify the particular real estate it is authorized to purchase? The answer is, no. In other words, the company is left in perfect freedom to operate in whatever building it sees fit, either to purchase new property or to purchase property in which they already operate.
Then, coming to the crux of the matter, the thing in which I was interested, I asked this direct question: Would it then be possible under this legislation to purchase a newspaper such as the Toronto Daily Star, and the answer was:	Legally, yes. There was
nothing to prevent it, but so far as he knew the company had no intention of so doing.
That is my argument for delay. I therefore move in amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe):
That section one be amended by deleting the words "one hundred thousand dollars" and substituting therefor the words "forty-five thousand dollars."
It will be noted that there is an extra $15,000, which represents a 50 per cent increase in rental value. I believe this might

be justified, until we have had some further opportunity to study the implications of this particular piece of legislation.

Mr. Chairman, this bill was fairly thoroughly examined in the committee on miscellaneous private bills. When I say that it was thoroughly examined, I mean there was an exhaustive discussion with respect to questions raised by various members of the committee. As the hon. member for Saskatoon City said a moment ago, I believe at the last meeting of the committee there were one or two questions which he had propounded earlier but which he did not follow up in the proceedings of the committee, perhaps because he was unable to be there.
In a moment I shall deal with the points involved. First, however, may I point out to him and the committee that there is nothing sinister in the bill now before us, nor is there anything in it which would in any way justify the suspicions expressed by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I do not wish to discuss in detail the questions he has raised, because in my view they are not relevant to the legislation before us. More than that I believe I could state properly that they are not based upon any inference which might properly be drawn from a piece of legislation as simple as this one.
I suppose it is always difficult in public affairs to separate what is taking place in two separate legislative bodies. Let me point out, however, that I believe the hon. member is carrying his inferences and his suspicions much too far, because if my memory serves me correctly this bill was introduced to the Senate some considerable time before any other bill, such as that which he has mentioned, was introduced in any other legislature.
As I pointed out on motion for second reading the purpose of this bill is a very simple one, and one which has nothing to do with the purchase of other properties. It has to do only with putting under one roof and into one company all the present establishment of the Globe and Mail which is published at the corner of King and York streets in Toronto. At the present time the building at that point, the real estate, is owned, and title to the land and building is in the name of the Mail Printing Company. Business is carried on under the name of the Globe Printing Company. All this bill attempts to do is simply to put both the business and the building and the real estate under the same name. I should not have thought anyone would raise any serious objection to that.

More than that, I think hon. members will readily understand that when companies are not incorporated by acts of parliament, similar to the original act in this case which was passed back in the sixties, no limitation is placed upon the value of property that a company can hold. The only limitation is that it be used for the purposes for which the charter provides. I suppose that, as we must come to parliament in these extraordinary circumstances of a statutory company, these questions may normally be raised.
I find no fault whatsoever with my hon. friend for raising any question because the committee desires to have a clear picture of exactly what is going on. I want to draw that picture just as clearly as I can. That being the case, I should like to point out to my hon. friend that if any purchase were contemplated this legislation would not be of any help. My little knowledge, and it is little, of how businesses as large as the figures *would indicate this one is are carried on is that this would not be of any assistance. I proffer that explanation from information I have received and which I believe is reliable.
I am anxious to give my hon. friend all the information there is at my disposal. When the company was first incorporated by statute in the sixties it was given the right to hold land to an annual rental value of $5,000. If my memory serves me correctly, in 1892 the company was given the right to increase its holdings of land to an annual value, which I think my hon. friend and I are in agreement as meaning a net rental value, of $30,000.
With the extension of the building and the erection of a structure such as this, and with costs being what they are, I would not think that even in the normal course of events an increase from $30,000 in those days to $100,000 would be much out of the way. The amendment now before us limits the increase to $45,000 and I would think that that is so restrictive as to make the bill practically useless. I am quite sure that my hon. friend has no desire to do that.
My hon. friend asked certain questions in the committee which I shall attempt to answer here. First, he asked the value of the property presently occupied by the Globe Printing Company, the title of which is in the name of the Mail Printing Company. This is the property the Globe Printing Company is attempting to get power to take over. I am told that the assessed value of the land and premises is $826,378 and the actual value of the property is said to be around $2 million. From the information given in the committee I would submit that the present request is not exorbitant nor are they going beyond the bounds of propriety when they ask for an annual value of $100,000.
29087-164i
Globe Printing Company
As a matter of fact this is a maximum amount. I fancy that the company is not desirous of coming back from time to time to ask for petty increases. Every opportunity was given before the committee for full disclosure, for full discussion and for full examination of all details of this transaction.
I think the further inquiry that the hon. member suggests should be made could have been made while the committee was sitting. At that time the representatives of the company, as members of the committee will testify, were ready to give every possible bit of information they could to the committee. I know of no information that was withheld.
For that reason I suggest that the amendment be not approved by this committee and that the original bill providing for an annual value of $100,000 be approved. I think that is a reasonable, proper and fit thing for this committee to do. This company should be given the right to purchase the property that it presently occupies.
Having had the circumstances detailed to him to the best of my knowledge I would ask the hon. member if he would not withdraw the amendment with the approval of his seconder and allow the bill to go through. I would not make that appeal if I had the slightest doubt as to the propriety of the legislation. More than that, if I had any doubt about it I would not be sponsoring the measure.
The hon. member gave a figure of $100,000; does that apply to the Mail Printing Company or the Globe Printing Company?
The assessed value of the property presently occupied by the Globe Printing Company is $826,378.
What did the $2 million figure represent?
The actual value of the property occupied by the Globe Printing Company is $2,031,516.
Is that the book value?
I cannot say as to that.
What are the corresponding figures for the Mail Printing Company?

The title of the building occupied by the Globe Printing Company is in the name of the Mail Printing Company. That information came out in the committee. I think I can satisfy my hon. friend by saying that the Mail Printing Company operates a small plant under lease in another part of the city where it carries on a job printing business.

I have heard the argument presented tonight by my hon. friend, just as

Globe Printing Company I heard what he had to say in the committee. While I am perfectly convinced of my hon. friend's personal integrity in the matter, nothing that he has said has made me change my mind in connection with the request I make that my amendment be voted on so that we may get the opinion of the members of this committee as to whether it would not be advisable to delay this legislation until we have some further information.

What objective can be gained by delaying the bill? This is an old company which was incorporated under letters of patent. A new company incorporated today would not be handicapped with this old shackle. The C.C.F. members are delaying the passage of the bill. Why will they not divulge their motive in asking for a delay? They have listened to this matter being discussed in committee. It has been hashed over time and time again. Yet they still contend that there is something wrong, something that is not quite correct. They are asking questions and they want to delay it. Why do they want to delay it? Why not let us see what they are driving at, or is it the fact that this bill concerns a private enterprise trying to carry on business? The C.C.F. members are spending the public's money at the rate of about $2,000 for every forty minutes. They have listened to this matter being hashed over time and again in committee, and nonsensically they are asking the same things again. It is utter nonsense.

Apparently somebody is not adhering strictly to the truth, because we have been told that we have heard this matter hashed over time and again in committee and yet the member for Saskatoon City has told us that he asked certain questions of counsel when the bill was before a committee of the house, and answers were not given. The member for Peel stated in his remarks that he would not go into the questions raised.
I did not say that.

You will And it in Hansard. I think it is only right that before we pass this legislation the committee should have some knowledge of what the facts are, and I believe these questions should be answered. That is all we are asking for now. There are no ulterior motives. I have no great regard, and less respect, for the Globe and Mail, but I am prepared to live and let live. As things are now, I do think that the committee is entitled to answers to the questions asked.

May I ask the hon. member if there are any questions that still remain unanswered? We have attempted to answer every single question that has been raised.

Mr. Speaker-
I put the motion.

The member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) raised a question as to the C.C.F. members obstructing the passage of the bill. He asked why they did not come out and state their real purpose in doing so. I think it is obvious from the remarks of the hon. member for Simcoe North that even in his own mind there must be something surrounding this whole matter that gives him the idea of suspicion about it. As far as I am concerned as a member of the house, I wish that a bill of this nature had not been introduced at this particular time. As to the member responsible for the introduction of the bill, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon),

I am quite ready to accept his word that the bill is just what he says it is. I do not know of any member of the house who commands the respect of other members more than the hon. member for Peel, and I take second place to no member of the house in my regard for his integrity. I am certain that he is of the opinion that this bill is the innocent little instrument that he claims it is.
Unfortunately I have a different feeling altogether about the bill. I cannot dissociate my mind, in considering this bill, from another bill that was introduced in another legislative chamber, that of the province of Ontario. I am certain that, if this particular bill that is now before the house had been introduced prior to discussion on that other bill in the legislature of the province of Ontario, members' minds would not be filled with doubt about the simplicity and the innocence of this bill. I think it is most unfortunate that the bill before the house is being introduced in such an unsavoury atmosphere. After all, this bill refers to a particular newspaper and a particular individual, who happens to be the owner and publisher of two newspapers in the city of Toronto. Those newspapers are wholehearted supporters of the party responsible for the introduction of this bill in this house and the other bill in the provincial legislature.
Order. I would ask the hon. member not to refer to an act which has been passed by a provincial house.

I accept your correction, Mr. Speaker; and if it had been made earlier I would have gladly observed your ruling at that time. In view of what was said by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson), since these thoughts were in my mind I could not help but feel that I should make myself clear to this house at any rate, so the hon. member would have no doubt about the position as far as I was concerned.
If I may interrupt, Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, would you be good enough to tell the house the rule which forbids us mentioning an act which has been passed by any of the nine provinces?
The hon. member knows quite well that this debate should be relevant to the bill now before the house. It has nothing to do with an act which has been passed by a provincial legislature.

I may not have heard correctly, but I understood you to make the observation that it was improper for the hon. member to refer to an act which had been passed by a provincial legislature. If I am in error I must apologize.
Globe Printing Company

I do not have them at hand just now, but I could give the hon. member rulings made by my predecessors to the effect that in this house we should not discuss legislation that has been passed by provincial legislatures.
What is the ruling now? We could not hear.

With great deference, Mr. Speaker, I accept your ruling, without regard to the point raised by the hon. member; and I shall continue on from there. If you will permit me to do so I should like to merely reiterate that my only purpose in making that observation was to perhaps enlighten the hon. member for Simcoe North, because I thought he asked the motive or purpose of hon. members of this party in delaying this bill, and I wanted to make my intentions quite clear.
I do not believe this bill should have third reading, and pass. I make that statement because ever since the inception of the newspaper now known as the Globe and Mail it has been able to carry on most competently and most efficiently. I make that statement knowing that I am paying a compliment to private enterprise, which hon. members to my right sometimes say we are not willing to do. I pay that compliment to the Globe and Mail, and I can do no less having in mind that I see this newspaper every morning about as well gotten up and as clean-perhaps not in its contents but at least in its appearance-as any newspaper published in Canada. It has been carrying on in this way ever since its inception. Two or three solicitors could have looked after that matter and saved much of that amount.
And going into western Canada, indicating the reason why our farmers complain, let me refer to the government elevator in the city of Saskatoon with a total capacity of 5,500,000 bushels. During the years 1947 and 1948 it was shown that the average use of this elevator in the first of those years was 52,071 bushels and in the other year 58,711 bushels. Without allowing anything for interest or any other charges of that nature, the cost of operating that elevator during the year, in salaries alone, amounted to $52,755 in each year, or 90 cents a bushel for every bushel of wheat stored in the elevator during the years 1947 and 1948.
I have various other examples before me which indicate that there has been gross extravagance on the part of this government.
In the speech from the throne we were apparently to be made aware of the defence measures taken by this country, and their adequacy. A steel program was to be brought before the house. We were promised amendments to the law regarding our armed forces. Amendments were to be made to the Industrial Development Bank Act, to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act; the shipbuilding industry was to receive assistance, the Department of Reconstruction and Supply was to be set up, and was to take over housing.
Some of these matters are on the order paper, and have been there for a period of
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker three or four weeks. What does all this add up to? There were so many matters in this legislative program as set out in the speech from the throne this year that the government must have intended that a normal session of parliament would be held.
The speech from the throne was a carryall of omnibus promises made to the Canadian people. When the speech from the throne was prepared the government had no idea of a short session. No government, having regard to this legislative program, could have anticipated or intended that at the end of two months the House of Commons would be dissolved.
Why this change? We welcome the change of heart, to give the Canadian people an opportunity of showing what they think about this government. In my opinion, this course is being followed not because the government wants to give the Canadian people that opportunity. What is the reason for this sudden haste, and the fact that this prospective legislation goes into the limbo of forgotten things?-except on the hustings, of course, when the forgotten items will be referred to. An endeavour will be made on the part of the government to say that they were obstructed; and I give them their answer now, that there has been no obstruction at this session and every piece of legislation that has been brought before the House of Commons has been passed. The charge of obstruction will provide no excuse. The reason the government now seeks to go to the country at this time lies in the fact that Canada's trade, both industrially and agriculturally, is in such a position that within the next two or three months this nation may face a national crisis such as we have not faced in many, many years.
I have before me a Canadian Press dispatch of April 14 which says:
Canada's favourable balance of trade with the rest of the world slumped sharply during February.
Reporting monthly trade totals, the bureau of statistics disclosed today that the favourable balance -the excess of exports over imports-fell to $1,200,000 in February from $15,200,000 in January and $28,100,000 in February, 1948.
. . . The downward trend resulted from a sudden substantial increase in the value of imports from other countries and a drop, though of smaller proportions, in sales to the export market.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was in British Columbia on April 14 he stated he realized the situation with regard to trade. Canada is faced with a trade peril, the like of which we in this nation have not faced for many years. In the speech from the throne we find this statement:
With a view to assisting in the restoration of world trade, so vital to general security and our own prosperity, Canada participated in formulating the

The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker
charter for the international trade organization and the general agreement on tariffs and trade which will be submitted for your approval.
Is there any member in the House of Commons who has heard a statement from any minister of the government in regard to trade, except the generalities which were indulged in by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech?
So far as agricultural trade is concerned, between 1939 and 1949 Canada negotiated 142 contracts for the supply of food products to the United Kingdom. We had as many as 22 in one year. Now we have three. Great Britain is entering into agreements everywhere in Europe. She has entered into negotiations for a five-year pact with Poland. She will get bacon, eggs and other food in return for wool, tin, copper, rubber and cotton. This trade agreement is expected in the five-year period to total $1,200 million. She would purchase from Russia 1,500,000 tons of corn, barley and oats during 1949. This would be twice as much as Russia sold Britain during 1948.
Britain has cut down her purchases of Canadian salmon, poultry, apples, beef, timber and newsprint. Now she takes less bacon and eggs. There is a picture which should demand and challenge the attention of the government at this time in this country.
Today in a Canadian Press dispatch from London the following appears:
United Kingdom bacon imports from Canada have slumped sharply in recent months. In February this year the United Kingdom took only 31,729 hundredweight, compared with 136,575 hundredweight in February, 1948-
-or approximately one-quarter of what the exports of bacon from Canada were one year ago. Our cheese contract is for less than we have had with the United Kingdom in a period of thirty years. It is true enough that the situation at the moment is being smoothed over by exports to the United States, but the similarity of our production with that of the United States and the agricultural surpluses that are being piled up there indicate the danger that is being faced by the Canadian farmer.
The same applies industrially and I would refer to that if I had more time at my disposal. I hold in my hand an advertisement that has appeared in the press this week with the picture of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) reading, "Our farmers have markets." That is what it says, but it could say something else. It could say that in 1941 there were 18 food contracts; in 1942, there were 14; in 1943 there were 15; in 1944 there were 19 as there were in 1945; in 1946 there were 22 and in 1949 there were three.
Our farmers face a situation in the matter of trade that is of serious consequence. The
[Mr. Diefenbaker.)

government realize that the accumulation of conditions will come to a head in the near future and instead of facing that issue before the people then they are attempting to run away from it through an election now.
The speech from the throne was filled to overflowing with everything that any minister could fondly imagine. It will be noted that legislation in the matter of social security which has been held up for years is being passed now and that in the last two or three days the overflowing heart of this government has been beating more rapidly for the people than ever before.
Defence matters and the other questions including the preservation of our trade are forgotten. They are hidden away and parliament is denied the opportunity of discussing them. The Canadian people are denied information or a solution for their trade plight. The reason for the haste can be explained in no other way. The Prime Minister has been across Canada; indeed while our markets tumbled, the Prime Minister traveled.

He was my seatmate for four years, and those were his beliefs. When speaking to the Rotary club of Montreal on April 20 on this business of co-operative or government enterprise, he said that in his own province they were operating a telephone service, an electric service, a bus transportation system and were also in timber, furs and insurance. Only one of the eleven government-owned firms, the tannery and shoe factory, had proved a failure; the other ten had shown profits of $5 million in 1947 and $3,132,000 in 1948. Then this newspaper report goes on:
"We are not suggesting we have the answer to all our social and economic problems," Premier Douglas concluded, "but we are seeking the answer."
He told them there, mind you, that since 1947 he went back to the extent of approximately $2 million. He also told them he did not consider that they had all the answers, but that they were seeking the answers.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He was in New York trying to borrow money.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He is forced to do that by the present federal government; and until such time as we all honestly seek the answers we are going to have the kind of skulduggery that we are experiencing today. Then, speaking in his own legislature in February, Douglas said practically the same thing. He said:
Of those businesses which have already been set up, I want to explain frankly that three of them, accounting for five per cent of the capital investment in crown companies, are problem children.
These are the fish board, tannery and shoe factory and the woollen mill. Another six, accounting for seven per cent of the investment, have yet to prove themselves. And seven, accounting for 88 per cent of investment, have definitely proved successful.
Well, is that not the experience in all business? There are ups and downs; there is a greater demand and a greater market for a certain product, and a greater mark-up on some than on others. The lesson to learn here is that if the fish board did not measure up to expectations it was because the fish in the inland lakes did not prove marketable in the United States. The woollen mill was a crown 
company set up where nothing existed before. I would like to ask my hon. friends if that was not a better experiment than slave camps for the unemployed at 20 cents a day. It was a case of trying that sort of thing, using the resources of the province to enable people to go to work and earn a dollar honestly and retain their dignity rather than seeking relief or the other ways out which cause our people to become demoralized.

speechtext: Why didn't he keep them going?

You would not know even if I were there. The thing that I cannot understand is why we should have a lack of markets in a basic industry in a province, at a time when we import so much coal from the United States. We imported coal to the value of $143 million last year at a time when we were producing a small amount of coal in Nova Scotia, with the mines working on half time. That is reminiscent of the thirties. Many people in that province cannot understand why this should be so. The only alibi offered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was, "Well, this has been a mild winter, and the railways are not burning as much coal". That is not an answer at all. It shows faulty planning. There is no plan to market the product of one of the basic industries, an industry which is basic to one province in this country.
I had intended to say more, but with the permission of the house I should like to make one observation with regard to steel. In my view the Minister of Trade and Commerce before dissolution of this parliament should

clarify the position of steel in Canada. The speech from the throne indicates that the government was anxious to expand that industry. To that extent they were prepared to match dollar for dollar with the industry in any expansion program which might be undertaken.
The minister stated in reply to a question from myself a month or so ago that the only section of the industry which had made application for that grant was Stelco, and that neither Dosco nor Algoma-the other two basic industries in the country-had indicated whether they would make use of it or not.
In the last issue of the Financial Post there was a statement to the effect that steel was becoming more plentiful, and that to that extent the federal government was likely to withdraw the dollar for dollar proposal it had made for the purpose of expanding the steel industry. There is a large steel plant in my constituency, one which produces a large share of Canada's basic steel, and I should like to know from the minister before I leave Ottawa whether Dosco made any application to expand its plant on the basis set out in the speech from the throne and, if not, why not? I should like to know if there is any truth in the statement which appears in the Financial Post that the government may withdraw this program of financial support for the purpose of expanding the industry. I am concerned about it, because I fully believe that the only solution to the problem of Nova Scotia is the expansion of the steel industry at Sydney. It uses a large percentage of the coal produced in that province. Unless that steel industry is expanded, I do not see a bright future for the province.
Secondly, the iron ore deposits in Labrador and Ungava are most important to this country. I note that a large number of American investors are coming into that industry in eastern Canada. I believe that five of the directors of Dosco are Americans; they are buying heavily into that stock.
With the ore situation such as it is on the North American continent, I believe that in the not far distant future there will be shifts of major steel plants to the east coast. I suggest we should try to hold our own industries in this country, and utilize the iron ore deposits in Ungava and Labrador for the purpose of building this country into a great industrial nation, rather than allowing its resources to slip to the other side of the border.
I should be pleased if the Minister of Trade and Commerce would look at my remarks in Hansard, and before the session

closes make some kind of statement as to the future of steel, particularly in the matter of expansion. May I thank the house for listening patiently at this time.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
